strings.name: Francia Márquez
strings.role: Former vice-president of Colombia and advocate for environmental and community rights
strings.summary: Francia Márquez entered national politics through community organising and campaigns against illegal gold mining in Cauca, winning the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2018. She served as Colombia’s vice-president from 2022 to 2026, becoming the first Afro-Colombian woman in that office, and concurrently served as the first minister of equality and equity from 2023 to 2025. Her political career connects environmental protection, ethnic representation and social equality.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026, including her interview of 21 August after leaving office. Reporting on 28 September described a possible Cali mayoral bid as unconfirmed; it does not establish a declared candidacy. Subsequent political activities and project developments require updating.
strings.influence.rationale: Her move from grassroots environmental and community-rights activism to Colombia’s vice-presidency increased political representation for Afro-descendant and disadvantaged communities.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and community background
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 1 December 1981 in Suárez, Cauca, Colombia, she grew up in Yolombó, in the La Toma area. Her early life was closely connected to the local Afro-Colombian community’s farming, artisanal gold mining and river environment.
strings.facts.f2.label: Legal education
strings.facts.f2.value: She graduated from the law programme at Universidad Santiago de Cali in 2020. Before gaining her university qualification, she had already participated in environmental and community-rights campaigns in her home region.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Environmental protection and ancestral land rights
strings.highlights.h1.text: She organised women around the Ovejas River and La Toma community against destructive illegal gold mining. The Goldman Environmental Prize recognised her organising and contribution to the removal of illegal mining equipment; those historical achievements do not mean that local pollution or mining problems have been permanently resolved.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Political representation and the challenges of governing
strings.highlights.h2.text: Her vice-presidency increased Afro-Colombian women’s representation in national politics. She promoted the creation of the Ministry of Equality and Equity, while facing institution-building difficulties and public disagreements with Petro. After leaving office, she expressed a wish to continue community work and described racism she had experienced within government.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Ends her vice-presidential term
strings.timeline.t1.text: She left office at the end of the Petro administration. In an interview on 21 August, she reflected on four years in government and outlined plans to return to social activism, write memoirs and establish a foundation; these plans should not be treated as completed projects.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Ends her service as equality and equity minister
strings.timeline.t2.text: Her ministerial handover report records 3 March as her departure date, with Carlos Rosero succeeding her. The cabinet announcement of 27 February had publicly signalled the change earlier. She continued as vice-president, so the two offices had different terms.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Sworn in as the first minister of equality and equity
strings.timeline.t3.text: At a ceremony in Manaure, La Guajira, she assumed leadership of the new ministry, serving women, young people, ethnic minorities and other excluded groups. The January law establishing the ministry, her designation on 29 June and the oath on 30 June mark separate institutional and appointment stages.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Sworn in as vice-president of Colombia
strings.timeline.t4.text: During the presidential inauguration proceedings before Congress, newly inaugurated President Gustavo Petro administered her oath, making her Colombia’s first Afro-Colombian woman vice-president. The record confirms actual assumption of office, beyond nomination as a candidate.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Becomes Petro’s vice-presidential running mate
strings.timeline.t5.text: After placing second in the Historic Pact coalition’s primary on 13 March, she was selected as Petro’s running mate. The primary result, announcement of the ticket, subsequent national election and inauguration were separate stages.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Completes her university law studies
strings.timeline.t6.text: She graduated from Universidad Santiago de Cali’s law programme. The university’s alumni account confirms the year; this professional education extended her practical involvement in community environmental and land-rights issues.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Receives the Goldman Environmental Prize
strings.timeline.t7.text: She received that year’s South and Central America award for organising La Toma’s women against illegal gold mining and protecting ancestral land. This is a distinct environmental award, not a Nobel Prize category.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Organises a women’s march to Bogotá against illegal gold mining
strings.timeline.t8.text: She led approximately 80 women from Cauca towards the capital, drawing attention to river pollution and damage to community land. An agreement with the government to take action followed in December; the prize organisation records the subsequent removal or destruction of illegal equipment.
